lessons.title: What is React Native?
lessons.theory:
## Learn Once, Write Anywhere
Historically, if a company wanted a mobile app, they had to hire two entirely separate teams: Swift/Objective-C developers for iOS, and Java/Kotlin developers for Android. This was incredibly expensive and slow.

**React Native**, created by Facebook, changed the industry. It allows developers to write an app using JavaScript and the React framework, and deploy it to *both* iOS and Android from a single codebase.

Unlike older tools (like Cordova) that just wrapped a web page in a mobile frame, React Native actually compiles your JavaScript UI components into native iOS and Android UI elements. A `<View>` in React Native becomes a real `UIView` on iOS and a `ViewGroup` on Android, providing the true speed, feel, and performance of a native app.
lessons.instructions:
## Task: Map Web to Native
1. Create a dictionary that maps HTML web tags to React Native components
2. Map: div, span, input, button, img

lessons.title: View and Text
lessons.theory:
## The Building Blocks
If you come from web development, you are used to using HTML tags like `<div>`, `<span>`, and `<h1>`.

In React Native, there is no HTML or DOM. You cannot use a `<div>`. Instead, React Native provides primitive mobile components:
- `<View>` is the fundamental container (the equivalent of a `div`). It supports layout using Flexbox.
- `<Text>` is the only component that can contain text (like a `p` or `span`). If you try to put raw text inside a `<View>`, the app will crash.
- `<Image>` displays graphics.

```jsx
<View style={{ flex: 1, justifyContent: 'center' }}>
  <Text style={{ fontSize: 24 }}>Hello Mobile World!</Text>
</View>
```
All styling is done using JavaScript objects that look almost identical to CSS, making the transition for web developers extremely fast.

lessons.title: React Navigation
lessons.theory:
## Moving Between Screens
On a website, navigating to a new page involves the browser requesting a new URL. Mobile apps don't have URLs in the same way. They use **Stacks** and **Tabs**.

**React Navigation** is the industry-standard library for handling this in React Native.
- **Stack Navigator:** Imagine a stack of playing cards. When you tap a profile, a new screen slides in *on top* of the current screen. When you hit the physical 'Back' button, the top screen is popped off the stack, revealing the previous screen underneath.
- **Tab Navigator:** The persistent buttons at the bottom of the screen (e.g., Home, Search, Profile) that allow you to switch instantly between parallel stacks.

Managing the navigation state properly is crucial, otherwise users get trapped in endless stacks of screens.

lessons.title: Web APIs
lessons.theory:
## Fetching Data
Mobile apps are rarely standalone; they almost always need to talk to a backend server to get data (like fetching a feed of posts).

Fortunately, React Native provides the exact same **Fetch API** that standard web browsers use. You don't need to learn a complex mobile networking library.

```javascript
fetch('https://api.example.com/users')
  .then(response => response.json())
  .then(data => console.log(data))
  .catch(error => console.error(error));
```
You trigger these network calls exactly as you would in React web: usually inside a `useEffect` hook when a component first mounts, saving the resulting data into state variables to trigger a UI re-render.

lessons.title: AsyncStorage
lessons.theory:
## Local Persistence
When a user closes an app and reopens it, they shouldn't have to log in again. You need to save their session token directly onto the phone's hard drive.

In a web browser, you use `localStorage`. In React Native, you use **AsyncStorage**. 

AsyncStorage is a simple, unencrypted, asynchronous, persistent, key-value storage system. Because reading from the phone's flash memory takes time, all AsyncStorage methods return Promises, meaning you must use `await` when reading or writing data.

*Note:* Because it is unencrypted, you should never store passwords or credit card numbers in AsyncStorage. For highly sensitive data, you must use native iOS Keychain or Android Keystore libraries.

lessons.solution:
import asyncio

class MockAsyncStorage:
    def __init__(self):
        self.storage = {}
        
    async def set_item(self, key, value):
        # Simulate a small delay
        await asyncio.sleep(0.1)
        self.storage[key] = value
        
    async def get_item(self, key):
        await asyncio.sleep(0.1)
        return self.storage.get(key)

async def main():
    db = MockAsyncStorage()
    await db.set_item('@token', 'xyz_123')
    token = await db.get_item('@token')
    print("Retrieved Token:", token)

# Run the async function (simulate React Native environment)
asyncio.run(main())
lessons.hint: Use `async def` for functions and `await` when calling them. Use `.get(key)` for dictionary lookup.
lessons.rubric: Async functions implemented correctly and data is stored/retrieved.

lessons.title: Expo vs CLI
lessons.theory:
## The Great React Native Debate
When you start a React Native project, you face a major architectural choice: use the bare **React Native CLI**, or use **Expo**.

**Expo** is a framework built around React Native. It hides all the complex iOS and Android configuration files. You don't need to open Xcode or Android Studio. You can build an app and test it on your physical phone in 2 minutes. However, historically, if you needed a custom Bluetooth library that Expo didn't support, you were stuck.

**Bare CLI** gives you full control. You have the raw iOS and Android project folders and can inject custom Swift or Kotlin code whenever you want. However, upgrading versions is notoriously painful and requires deep native knowledge.

Today, Expo is so advanced (with features like Custom Dev Clients) that the official React Native documentation explicitly recommends using Expo for almost all new projects.

lessons.title: Bridging to Swift/Kotlin
lessons.theory:
## Touching the Metal
React Native covers 95% of what a mobile app needs. But sometimes you hit an edge case. Maybe you need to interface with a proprietary credit card swiper hardware that only provides a Swift and Kotlin SDK.

In this scenario, you write a **Native Module** (a Bridge).

You write the low-level Swift code to talk to the hardware on iOS. You then expose specific functions (like `swipeCard()`) to JavaScript via a bridging header. On the JavaScript side, you simply call `NativeModules.CardSwiper.swipeCard()`. This gives React Native the ultimate escape hatch: you get the speed of writing UI in JS, with the raw power of accessing any native device feature when necessary.
lessons.instructions:
## Task: Native Module Bridge Simulator
1. Simulate a JS call to a Native Android module.
2. In Python, create a JS environment that passes a message to an Android environment.
3. The Android environment processes it and returns a simulated Promise string.
lessons.starterCode:
class AndroidNativeModule:
    def get_battery_level(self):
        # Simulate native Java/Kotlin code reading hardware
        print("[Android Code executing...]")
        return 87 # 87%

class JSEnvironment:
    def __init__(self, native_module):
        self.native = native_module
        
    def check_battery(self):
        print("[JS] Requesting battery level over bridge...")
        # Call the native method
        level = self.___.___()
        print(f"[JS] Promise resolved: Battery is at {___}%")

# Setup
android_hardware = AndroidNativeModule()
react_app = JSEnvironment(android_hardware)

# Execute
react_app.check_battery()
lessons.solution:
class AndroidNativeModule:
    def get_battery_level(self):
        # Simulate native Java/Kotlin code reading hardware
        print("[Android Code executing...]")
        return 87 # 87%

class JSEnvironment:
    def __init__(self, native_module):
        self.native = native_module

# Setup

lessons.title: The JS Bridge
lessons.theory:
## How It Actually Works
How does JavaScript code written on a laptop tell an iPhone to render a physical button?

React Native runs two main threads concurrently: the **Main Thread** (which handles the native UI rendering and user touches) and the **JS Thread** (which runs your React logic).

They communicate across **The Bridge**. The JS Thread figures out that a button needs to be rendered, serializes that instruction into a JSON message, and shoots it across the Bridge to the Native thread. The Native thread reads the JSON and physically draws the button on the screen.

This architecture is why passing massive amounts of data back and forth across the bridge (like a 60fps video stream) causes lag. (Note: Modern React Native is currently rolling out the JSI architecture to replace the bridge, allowing direct synchronous memory access!).
lessons.instructions:
## Task: Bridge Bottleneck Simulator
1. Simulate the JS thread and the Native thread.
2. The bridge can only handle 5 messages per frame. If more are sent, it drops them.
3. Loop through 10 animation updates and see how many are dropped if sent over the bridge.
lessons.starterCode:
class JSBridge:
    def __init__(self):
        self.capacity_per_frame = 5
        
    def send_messages(self, num_messages):
        if num_messages > self.___:
            dropped = num_messages - self.___
            print(f"Warning: Bridge overloaded! Dropped {dropped} messages.")
            return self.capacity_per_frame
        return num_messages

bridge = JSBridge()

print("Sending 3 updates (Light load):")
processed = bridge.send_messages(3)
print(f"Processed: {processed}
")

print("Sending 10 updates (Heavy animation load):")
processed = bridge.send_messages(10)
print(f"Processed: {processed}")
lessons.solution:
class JSBridge:
    def __init__(self):
        self.capacity_per_frame = 5
        
    def send_messages(self, num_messages):
        if num_messages > self.capacity_per_frame:
            dropped = num_messages - self.capacity_per_frame
            print(f"Warning: Bridge overloaded! Dropped {dropped} messages.")
            return self.capacity_per_frame
        return num_messages

bridge = JSBridge()

print("Sending 3 updates (Light load):")
processed = bridge.send_messages(3)
print(f"Processed: {processed}
")

print("Sending 10 updates (Heavy animation load):")
processed = bridge.send_messages(10)
print(f"Processed: {processed}")
lessons.rubric: Bridge successfully processes 3 messages, but warns and drops 5 messages when given 10.

lessons.title: Widgets are Everything
lessons.theory:
## The Flutter Philosophy
While React Native uses React components, Google's **Flutter** takes a completely different approach: *Everything is a Widget*.

In Flutter, the app itself is a widget. The layout is a widget. The buttons are widgets. Even the padding and alignment are separate widgets. You build UIs by snapping together complex, deeply nested trees of widgets.

Unlike React Native (which uses native iOS/Android UI elements), Flutter has its own ultra-fast 2D rendering engine (Skia). Flutter draws every single pixel on the screen itself. This guarantees that an app looks 100% identical on an iPhone 15 and a 5-year-old Android phone, but it means it bypasses the native OS UI components entirely.

## Task: Create a Text Widget
Return a simple Text widget with the string 'Hello Flutter' centered on the screen.
lessons.rubric: Correctly instantiates the Text widget with the string.

lessons.title: Stateful vs Stateless
lessons.theory:
## Managing Component Memory
In mobile development (whether React Native or Flutter), components fall into two categories: Stateful and Stateless.

- **Stateless Components** are dumb. You pass them data (Props), and they render it. If the data doesn't change, they don't change. A static Header or a custom Button is usually stateless.
- **Stateful Components** have memory. They hold variables (State) that change over time, like the text in a search input, or a boolean tracking if a modal is open or closed.

Whenever the 'State' of a component changes, the framework automatically re-renders that component (and its children) to reflect the new data. Managing exactly *when* and *why* state changes is the hardest part of mobile architecture.

lessons.title: Redux Toolkit
lessons.theory:
## The Heavyweight Champion
For massive enterprise applications, **Redux Toolkit (RTK)** remains the industry standard for global state management.

Redux enforces a very strict, predictable architectural pattern:
1. **State:** A single, massive JSON object holding all app data.
2. **Actions:** If a component wants to change data, it cannot modify it directly. It must 'dispatch' an Action (a description of what happened, e.g., 'ADD_TO_CART').
3. **Reducers:** Pure functions that receive the Action, calculate the new state, and return a brand new State object.

While traditional Redux required hundreds of lines of boilerplate code, Redux Toolkit streamlines this massively, automatically configuring the store and providing tools for efficient API caching (RTK Query).

lessons.title: Requesting Permissions
lessons.theory:
## Respecting User Privacy
Mobile operating systems heavily restrict what an app can do. If your app needs the camera, location, or microphone, it will crash if it tries to access them without permission.

In React Native, you must explicitly ask the user for permission using the OS prompts.

For iOS, you must add specific keys to your `Info.plist` file (e.g., `NSCameraUsageDescription`), explaining exactly *why* you need the camera. If you don't provide a good reason, Apple will reject your app during the App Store review. In the code, you use libraries like `expo-location` or `react-native-permissions` to trigger the popup, check if the user said 'Yes', and gracefully handle the scenario where they say 'No'.

## Task: Expo Notifications

lessons.title: Handling Foreground Messages
lessons.theory:
## Push Notifications
Push Notifications are critical for retaining users. They involve three parties: Your app, Your Backend Server, and APNs/FCM (Apple/Google notification services).

When a user installs your app, it requests a unique **Push Token** from Apple/Google. Your app sends this token to your backend database.

When your backend wants to alert the user, it sends a message (containing the token) to Apple/Google's servers, which then wake up the physical phone. 

Handling notifications is tricky because behavior changes based on app state. If the app is in the **Background/Closed**, the OS displays a standard banner popup. But if the app is in the **Foreground** (currently open and being used), the OS usually blocks the banner. You have to write custom code to intercept the foreground message and show a custom in-app toast notification.
lessons.instructions:
## Task: Notification Listener
Set up a listener to console log the notification when received in the foreground.
lessons.rubric: Correctly attaches the notification listener.

lessons.title: AsyncStorage / SQLite
lessons.theory:
## Offline-First Architecture
Users expect mobile apps to open instantly and work even when they are on a subway with no cellular connection. This requires an **Offline-First** architecture.

Instead of fetching data from the internet every time the app opens, the app reads data from a local database instantly. 
- For simple key-value pairs (like user settings), use **AsyncStorage**.
- For complex relational data (like thousands of chat messages or a product catalog), you use a local **SQLite** database built directly into the phone.

When the internet connection returns, a background sync engine silently reaches out to your API, pulls down any new data, updates the local SQLite database, and the UI automatically re-renders with the fresh data.
lessons.instructions:
## Task: Save to AsyncStorage
Write the function to save a string value to AsyncStorage.
lessons.rubric: Correctly calls setItem with the key and value.

lessons.title: Sync Queues
lessons.theory:
## Making Changes Offline
What happens if a user 'Likes' a post while they are offline on a subway?

The app shouldn't show an error. Instead, it uses a **Sync Queue** (optimistic UI updates). 

1. The app immediately updates the local UI (turning the heart red) so the user feels it worked instantly.
2. It writes a 'Like Post ID 123' task into a local Queue table in SQLite.
3. The app listens for the OS network status to change to 'Online'.
4. Once online, a background worker reads the Queue and attempts to send the API request to the backend. 
5. If the server is down, the task stays in the queue and retries later using exponential backoff.
lessons.instructions:
## Task: NetInfo Check
Use the NetInfo library to check if the device is connected before attempting a sync.
lessons.rubric: Checks if the state isConnected.

lessons.title: Fastlane Basics
lessons.theory:
## Automating Mobile Releases
Building and releasing mobile apps is a miserable, manual process. You have to increment version numbers, generate cryptographic signing certificates, take screenshots, build the `.ipa` (iOS) and `.apk` (Android) files, and manually upload them to the Apple and Google portals.

**Fastlane** is an open-source tool written in Ruby that automates this entire process. 

You define a `Fastfile`. With a single command in your terminal (`fastlane deploy`), Fastlane automatically increments the build number, signs the app, builds the binaries, uploads them to TestFlight and the Google Play Console, and even posts a message in your team's Slack channel saying the new beta is ready.
lessons.instructions:
## Task: Fastfile Lane
Define a fastlane 'lane' named 'beta' that builds the iOS app and uploads it to TestFlight.
lessons.starterCode:
lane :___ do
  build_app(workspace: "MyApp.xcworkspace", scheme: "MyApp")
  upload_to____
end
lessons.solution:
lane :beta do
  build_app(workspace: "MyApp.xcworkspace", scheme: "MyApp")
  upload_to_testflight
end
lessons.rubric: Defines the beta lane and uploads to testflight.

lessons.title: EAS Build (Expo)
lessons.theory:
## Compiling in the Cloud
If you use Expo, you don't even need Fastlane or a powerful Mac. Expo provides **EAS (Expo Application Services)**.

Historically, to compile an iOS app, you absolutely had to own an Apple Mac computer to run Xcode. With EAS Build, you run `eas build --platform ios` in your terminal. 

Expo zips up your JavaScript code, uploads it to their massive server farm of Macs in the cloud, compiles the native iOS and Android binaries for you, and gives you a link to download the finished app. It handles all the nightmare-inducing Apple certificates and provisioning profiles automatically.

## Task: EAS Config
Define the eas.json build profile for production to auto-increment the build number.
lessons.rubric: Sets autoIncrement to boolean true.

Flutter Framework Masterclass.aiRubric: Assess deep understanding of Flutter and Dart

lessons.title: Everything is a Widget
lessons.theory:
## The Building Blocks of Flutter
To reiterate a core concept of Flutter: Everything is a widget. 

In Android or iOS native development, an application, a layout, and a button are fundamentally different types of software objects. In Flutter, they all inherit from the exact same Widget class.

If you want to center text, you don't apply a CSS style. You wrap the `Text` widget inside a `Center` widget. If you want padding, you wrap it in a `Padding` widget. This compositional approach results in deeply nested code (the infamous 'Widget Tree'), but provides unparalleled flexibility because you can combine widgets in infinite ways.
lessons.instructions:
## Task: Base Class

# Options: StatelessWidget, StatefulWidget, InheritedWidget
base_class = '___'
lessons.solution:

base_class = 'StatefulWidget'
lessons.hint: It needs state, so it's a StatefulWidget
lessons.rubric: Identifies StatefulWidget.

lessons.title: Dart Language Basics
lessons.theory:
## Google's Alternative to JavaScript
To write Flutter apps, you must learn **Dart**. Dart is an object-oriented, strongly typed language created by Google. 

If you know Java, C#, or JavaScript, Dart will feel instantly familiar. It was designed to be easy to learn and highly optimized for building user interfaces.

Dart has a killer feature called **Sound Null Safety**. In older languages (like Java), any variable could unexpectedly be `null`, leading to the infamous 'Null Pointer Exception' crashing the app. In Dart, variables cannot be null by default. If a variable *might* be null, you must explicitly declare it with a question mark (e.g., `String? name`). The compiler then forces you to write code handling the null case before it allows the app to compile, eliminating an entire category of crashes.
lessons.instructions:
## Task: Nullable Types
Declare a String variable named `username` that is allowed to be null.
lessons.starterCode: String___ username = null;
lessons.solution: String? username = null;
lessons.rubric: Uses String?.

lessons.title: Layouts in Flutter
lessons.theory:
## Rows and Columns
Flutter does not use CSS or Flexbox (like React Native does). Instead, layout is entirely managed by layout widgets, primarily **Rows** and **Columns**.

- A **Column** arranges its children vertically.
- A **Row** arranges its children horizontally.

To control spacing, you use properties like `MainAxisAlignment` (how children are distributed along the primary axis) and `CrossAxisAlignment`. 

If the items inside a Column are too tall and go off the screen, Flutter will throw a bright yellow warning tape error on the screen. To fix this, you don't add CSS overflow properties; you simply wrap the Column in a `SingleChildScrollView` widget, instantly making it scrollable.

lessons.title: Animations in Flutter
lessons.theory:
## Built-In Brilliance
Animations are where Flutter absolutely outshines every other framework. Because Flutter controls the 2D rendering engine directly, creating complex 60fps animations is astonishingly easy.

Flutter provides **Implicit Animations**. You don't have to manage math or animation controllers. You simply swap a standard widget for an animated one. 

For example, instead of a `Container`, you use an `AnimatedContainer`. If you change its width from 100 to 200 based on state, you don't just see it snap to 200. The `AnimatedContainer` automatically interpolates the values and smoothly animates the width change over a specified duration. For more complex, character-based animations, Flutter integrates flawlessly with Rive and Lottie.

  color: isBlue ? Colors.blue : Colors.red,

lessons.title: Publishing to App Stores

## The Final Hurdle
The hardest part of mobile development is often just getting the app approved and published.

**Google Play Store:** Generally lenient. You pay a one-time $25 fee. The review process takes a few days. The biggest hurdle for new accounts is Google's recent rule requiring you to find 20 real people to test your app for 14 continuous days before they allow you to publish it to production.

**Apple App Store:** Extremely strict. You must pay $99 every single year. The app is reviewed by human testers who will ruthlessly reject it if it crashes, uses private APIs, has a poor user interface, or tries to bypass Apple's 30% payment cut. You must provide test accounts and detailed explanations of every permission you use.
